Even lying down, Ms. Chenoweth -- who performed similar magic in ''You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown'' four years ago (and won a Tony) -- remains airborne, proving that in the perilous skies of Broadway, nothing can top undiluted star power as aviation fuel.
“Wicked” boasts ugly costumes, ugly choreography and an ugly set by Eugene Lee.
With her knockout star turn in "Wicked," Kristin Chenoweth establishes herself as the most bewitching musical-comedy actress of her generation.
A strenuous effort to be all things to all people tends to weigh down this lumbering, overstuffed $14 million production.
One can see where the $14 million went, though one cannot applaud their sense of direction.

A marvel of organization and inventiveness. Lusciously composed, smartly written and beautifully staged, 'Wicked' is one of the rare shows in town that justifies a $100 ticket. The cost is easily paid back in memories alone.
In toto (we couldn’t resist), there are so many wonderful things in Wicked that to dismiss it — as so many critics have done — strikes us as perverse.
The latest incarnation of this impeccably oiled entertainment machine finds a new gear courtesy of a British import.

It's safe to say that this is the most complete, and completely satisfying, new musical I've come across in a long time...Wicked offers a post-feminist, socially conscious reinterpretation of the story of Oz's Wicked Witch of the West...A fine ensemble helps ensure that even the most flagrantly cute and sentimental moments are hard to resist.
Wicked works because it has something Broadway musicals have largely given up on: a story that adults can take seriously.
Everything looks so tangible, touchable, that that in and of itself turns the production into an argument for live theater.
I know I’ve nit-picked, and though there are nits to pick, it’s time for me to say “Wick-KEDDD” in a guttural voice that conveys a good deal of respect.

"'Wicked' tries, in its ambition, to do so much that it's inevitable that it fails to be a smooth, cohesive show. It's too long - two-hours-45- minutes - and it often has a lumbering quality. But its reach, its attempt to be meaty and relevant and theatrical, is not only admirable, it's stimulating.
Perhaps that’s the ultimate takeaway from this musical — that lack of concern is the most wicked feeling of them all.

While Wicked could not exist without Baum's classic tale this new musical's real inspirational source is Gregory Maguire's cleverly conceived and executed novel Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West.

Ruth Westheimer in a new one-woman show (click on the links below for full reviews): Becoming Dr. Ruth Debra Jo Rupp arrives to the NYC stage in a 100-minute bioplay about everyone’s favorite cuddly German sex therapist, accent and all. Was it better than a good shag?
The problem with the show's book is that it has to cover so much ground in a connect-the-dots fashion that we're deprived of the necessary depth and character development.
The special effects were impressive but a show of this caliber needed more.

The new musical at the Gershwin is a thoroughly mechanical and unmagical musical. It is the ultimate whitewashed example of how a musical written to pander can even fail at that when it has no centralized guiding force.
Nothing about "Wicked" is magical.
Hence Wicked, a hideous mess of a musical that wants to be many different things, and rarely succeeds in being any of them.
I’m in love with this show; I’m in love with the message it sends and the lesson that there is perhaps wickedness thrust upon good people at times.

This show is amazing and I highly recommend it to anyone who ever loved the Wizard of Oz, who loves broadway, who loves singing and dancing and loves to see a full stage of special effects, detailed costumes and an overall great show.
It is an incredibly successful merging of dramatic spectacle and character development - and is one of the few truly unforgettable moments I have seen in a Broadway musical.

Whenever she opens her mouth - whether to demonstrate her supple coloratura or to detonate a verbal grenade or two - 'Wicked' makes endearingly whimsical noises, the sounds of a bona fide crowd-pleaser.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this lavish spectacle, praising Chenoweth's star turn and Schwartz's score while faulting its overstuffed book and muddled tone. Despite mixed reviews, most agree the $14 million production delivers enough magic to enchant audiences.

sg.ra: In a 1,933-seat house (the largest on Broadway), mid-orchestra is where the math works: far enough back that Wicked's dragon and flying monkeys clear the top of the frame, but close enough that you still catch faces. Every guide converges on rows F-L as the sweet spot (TickPick, RateYourSeats, Broadway.com), and a Fodor's veteran names 'Row H, as close to center as possible' as the ideal. Critically, the mezz overhang only starts around Orchestra Row N/O (SeatPlan, TickPick), so Row H is fully out from under it — you retain full vertical clearance for aerial scenery that rear-orchestra seats partially lose.

The Gershwin's proscenium is scaled for a 1,933-seat house, and Wicked's signature moments — the mechanical dragon perched above the arch, flying monkeys in Act 1, Elphaba's levitation in 'Defying Gravity' — play vertically as much as horizontally. Front orchestra loses all of that to the angle above your head (a Row BB seat reported only seeing 'blinding light' when Elphaba rises). Front mezzanine C is the reframe: SeatPlan calls the center front row 'the best view at this level,' Broadway.com recommends the first two mezz rows for spectacle shows, and a Tripadvisor advisor notes front mezz 'is actually a little closer than Orchestra Row O.' You trade facial detail for a complete aerial frame. Note: a low safety bar sits in front of Row A, an issue for short patrons (Broadway.com).

Because Gershwin is the largest house on Broadway, the rear mezzanine's back rows are genuinely farther from the stage than most theatres' comparable seats. AViewFromMySeat user reports in Rear Mezz L-113 call it 'very far away,' Rear Mezz M-11 calls it 'second to last row — it's very far away and hard to make out exact features of the actors,' Rear Mezz J-29 notes 'the stage is quite far away, so I couldn't see their expressions.' SeatPlan corroborates: rear mezz seats 'a considerable distance from the stage, so it may not be possible to make out facial expressions.' Sound gets good reviews back here (multiple comments note 'sound was amazing'), but for a character-driven show the resolution collapse is real. If price is the only consideration, the mid-rear-mezz rows (F-H) sit closer and perform far better.

TickPick calls this out directly: 'Orchestra Right (even-numbered side), above Row G... you won't miss a thing. In terms of price, you probably won't find a better deal on Wicked Tickets than the partially obstructed view seats.' What you miss on the Left orchestra side is 'a metal dragon' — a decorative element, not live action (TickPick). An AViewFromMySeat user in Orch L row J seats 25/27, sold as partial view, confirms: 'you could see everything but part of the house scenery but no action! Very close and could see facial expressions perfectly!' The value play is real because the discount is priced against a worst-case reading of 'obstructed,' but above Row G the obstruction is almost entirely non-action scenery. Rule of thumb from TickPick: prefer lower seat numbers (closer to the center aisle) within this range — e.g. seat 15 in Row O over seat 17 in Row N.

Gershwin's rear orchestra transitions into stadium-style seating around Row Q — an AViewFromMySeat user in Orch R Row T-32 writes 'Row Q and up are on a steeper incline which is great if you're short like me. Seats were also cheaper!' Another in Orch C Row V-116 notes 'back of orchestra is stadium seating so everything is still very visible. Still feels close given how far back it is.' SeatPlan confirms 'stadium seating on the Orchestra level refers to rows Q-Z.' These rows sit under the mezzanine overhang (TickPick: Front Mezz Row A overhangs Orch Row O; SeatPlan: begins at Row N), which clips the very top of tall scenery — a real trade for Wicked's dragon — but the steep rake solves the biggest problem of a 1,933-seat house: getting a clear sightline over the person in front of you. For short patrons specifically, this section over-performs its price tier.
